text: Every speaker, in your phone or in a concert hall, is built from the same few parts. The blueprints are on file.
April, eighteen seventy-four. Werner Siemens files a patent for a coil of wire, suspended in the narrow gap of a magnet. Alternating currents, he writes, cause the coil to vibrate up and down.
April, nineteen twenty-five. At General Electric, Chester Rice fixes the coil to a diaphragm of conical form, and adds a spider, to stop the coil moving sideways in the gap.
By nineteen forty-four, the cone's edge sat on a corrugated rim. At R C A, Harry Olson files a softer one, for deeper bass.
A modern speaker goes together in roughly that order. Magnet. Frame. Spider. The coil into the gap. The cone. The surround.
One idea, over a hundred and fifty years old. Current, in a coil, in a magnet, moving air.
